metadata.title: Defense-tech tester Valkryn emerges with $17 million

content.text:
Valkryn exited stealth with $17 million raised and a workforce with ties to some of America's buzziest businesses — including Applied Intuition, Palantir Technologies and SpaceX.
Why it matters: The Washington-based startup wants to help call the balls and strikes of defense tech by serving as a neutral auditor of the robotic and autonomous systems troops are increasingly wielding (and being threatened by).
-
"Test is scarce. It's really hard to do. It's really rare to do," co-founder Hugh Zabriskie told Axios.
-
"Companies wait months for an opportunity to demonstrate themselves," he said. "There's a lot of talk about being more adaptable and moving faster. Ultimately, that is on the back of test capacity, proving capacity."
State of play: Valkryn today is advertising:
-
"Battle Lab" technology, which instruments real-world tests of autonomous systems under realistic combat conditions and measures how they perform.
-
Quickly available test records and scoring measured against government criteria to help officials figure out which UAV, UGV or USV is the best fit.
"The reason there is often such a large gap between claimed performance — I'm sure you've seen this — and real performance is that there is such a lack of ability to understand that performance in the first place," Zabriskie said.
-
"We primarily operate on the fact that the government already has a massive outlay of land and airspace, and this is a resource that is fundamentally underutilized."
Between the lines: This all hinges on an unbiased track record — plus test, evaluation and training dollars.
-
"Neutral means we don't build the systems that are under test," Zabriskie said.
The intrigue: Valkryn recently worked with a task force in the Middle East. Additional details are scarce.
Follow the money: The startup's $15 million seed was led by Andreessen Horowitz. Ambition Capital, Caffeinated Capital and Cantos Ventures participated.
-
It previously raised a $2 million pre-seed.
The bottom line: "With this growing ocean of robotic and autonomous systems, we're reaching a breaking point," Zabriskie said.
-
"Traditional testing is very event-based and waterfall-based," he added. "The future is very clearly continuous."
